title: Improved IoT Sensors Data Quality for Smart Aquaponics Yield Prediction
author: Eneh, Udanor, et al.
materials: sensor based aquaponics fish pond datasets

steps.title: Prepare experimental ponds
steps.instruction: Set up twelve tarpaulin fish ponds on the university campus; allocate nine ponds for IoT sensor units with plant beds and three ponds as controls without sensors or plants. In each farmer site, install three ponds, one with IoT units only, one with IoT units plus plant beds, and one control pond.

steps.title: Assemble original IoT sensor unit
steps.instruction: Construct the first IoT system using a 32‑bit ESP‑32 microcontroller (with built‑in Wi‑Fi), connect six water‑quality sensors (four submersible: temperature, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, pH; two gas: ammonia (MQ‑137) and nitrate (MQ‑135) suspended above water), calibrate them, and program data acquisition.

substeps.instruction: Calibrate each sensor according to manufacturer specifications; use calibration solutions such as sodium hydroxide for the pH and dissolved‑oxygen sensors.
Wire the sensors to the ESP‑32 I/O pins (temperature DS18B20 to digital pin 2; the remaining sensors to appropriate analog pins).

Write C code in the Arduino IDE version 1.8.4 (Sketch) to read all six parameters and upload them via the ESP‑32 Wi‑Fi module to the Thingspeak IoT cloud (channel https://thingspeak.com/channels/1414062/) every 18 seconds, the minimum interval allowed by Thingspeak.
Power the unit with a 5 V supply and verify continuous data transmission for a short test period.

steps.title: Evaluate first system performance
steps.instruction: Run the original system for ten months, compare sensor outputs with ground‑truth measurements, and note that the pH sensor and both gas sensors (MQ‑135, MQ‑137) gave unreliable high or erratic values, especially the pH sensor which was unsuitable for the pond volume.

steps.title: Redesign IoT hardware
steps.instruction: Build an improved system using an Arduino Mega 2560 + Wi‑Fi R3 (with embedded ESP8266), a professional-grade pH meter suitable for large water volumes, and a MICS‑6814 multi‑gas sensor for ammonia and nitrite detection.

substeps.instruction: Note hardware specs: voltage range 5‑12 V, flash memory up to 32 MB, CPU speed up to 80 MHz, 54 digital pins (15 PWM), 16 analog inputs, and four UART ports.
The MICS‑6814 detects CO (1‑1000 ppm), NO₂ (0.05‑10 ppm), ethanol (10‑500 ppm), H₂ (1‑1000 ppm), NH₃ (1‑500 ppm), CH₄ (>1000 ppm), C₃H₈ (>1000 ppm), and C₄H₁₀ (>1000 ppm).

steps.title: Wire sensors to Arduino Mega
steps.instruction: Connect each sensor to the specified pins on the Arduino Mega 2560 + Wi‑Fi:

substeps.instruction: DS18B20 temperature sensor → digital pin 2.
Total dissolved solids (TDS) sensor → analog pin A0.
pH sensor → analog pin A1.
Dissolved‑oxygen sensor → analog pin A2.
Nitrate gas sensor → analog pin A4.
Ammonia gas sensor → analog pin A5.
Turbidity sensor → analog pin A6.
Water‑level sensor → analog pin A7.

steps.title: Program improved microcontroller
steps.instruction: Write C code in Arduino IDE 1.8.4 to read all eight analog inputs and the digital temperature input, then transmit the six water‑quality parameters (temperature, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, pH, ammonia, nitrate) to the Thingspeak channel every 18 seconds.

substeps.instruction: Include Wi‑Fi connection handling via the ESP8266 module.
Implement error checking and reconnection logic for the GSM router gateway.
Upload the compiled sketch to the Arduino Mega 2560.

steps.title: Calibrate improved sensors
steps.instruction: Perform calibration of each sensor according to industry standards:

substeps.instruction: Use appropriate calibration solutions (e.g., sodium hydroxide) for the pH and dissolved‑oxygen sensors.
Follow the MICS‑6814 datasheet to set baseline readings for ammonia and nitrite.
Record calibration curves and store them in the microcontroller firmware.

steps.title: Deploy units and collect data
steps.instruction: Install the calibrated IoT units in the designated ponds (nine university ponds and the farmer ponds with sensors), power them, and start continuous real‑time data acquisition and cloud upload as programmed.
